footer: Full-course recap for DSM-109 Mathematical Programming, S1–S9 (Prof. Amit Kumar Vatsa). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. Every corner point, shadow price, allowable range and reduced cost on this page was recomputed with scipy.optimize.linprog and matches the lecture and Excel Solver figures. The widgets replay the lecture's own models: the furniture LP, Merton Truck (Models 101/102/103 and overtime), Red Brand Canners, and the S8–S9 shadow-price and duality examples.
course_notes: Central contrast: amber = the model / the answer (formulation, feasible region, corner point, optimal plan, primal); teal = the insight the instructor says matters more than the answer (shadow price, allowable increase/decrease, reduced cost, dual). The instructor repeats 'the optimal solution is not the most interesting part; the insights are.' The S9 quiz is pen-and-paper, MCQ plus small numericals, and WILL ask the graphical method — so the graphical lab is the centrepiece; one line about the quiz format is allowed in module 3. Money: USD for Merton and Red Brand, rupees for the flight puzzle. Write 'Merton Truck' (ASR garbled it). The case 'Red Brand Canners'.

modules.plan: Module 'Why OR, and why not brute force' (S1–S2). Cheat cards: OR = applying analytical methods to decisions (name from WWII military operations; Dantzig, simplex); convex vs non-convex (local = global only in convex); growth: n! (assignment, TSP), 2^n (subset-sum truck loading, sum of C(n,k) = 2^n - 1); the 'computing power doubles' table; assignment problem as LP has the integrality property (Simplex LP gives 0/1 without declaring binary) while subset-sum needs binary variables and is NP-hard; LP relaxation first, branch and bound; why LP is popular (applicable, Karmarkar polynomial time, insights). Notes/analogies (cite sessions): Enigma 26^10 and the weather-report crib (S1); airline single price p* = a/2b and price discrimination / Surf Excel variants, JIT vs EOQ — 'don't get absorbed in the math and miss the bigger picture' (S1); the five-week flight puzzle: 40k -> 34k -> 30k, the lower-bound argument 10 legs / 2 x 6000, 'a guarantee of optimality is priceless', alternate optima exist (S1); dozers: greedy 190 km vs 150 km optimal, ~21% (S1); chessboard and wheat: 'think about the last square' (S2); 50! on an exaflop machine outlives the universe (S1). ONE widget: 'doubling slider' — choose growth class (log n, n, n^2, 2^n, n!) and number of doublings of computing power (0-10); readout shows the new solvable size starting from n = 100, with a small bar or table comparing all five classes; caption: four years of hardware gives exponential exactly one more city. Worked problems: flight puzzle lower bound; subset-sum count 2^n - 1 for n = 10 (1023).
modules.facts: Doubling once from n=100: log n -> 10,000; n -> 200; n^2 -> 141 (100*sqrt2 = 141.4); 2^n -> 101; n! -> stays 100 (101! = 101*100! needs 101x the compute). General after d doublings: log: 100^(2^d); linear: 100*2^d; quadratic: 100*2^(d/2); exponential: 100+d; factorial: largest n with n!/100! <= 2^d. 26^10 ≈ 1.41e14. 50! ≈ 3.04e64; at 1e18/s that is ≈ 9.6e38 years; universe ≈ 1.4e10 years. 20! ≈ 2.43e18. Chessboard total 2^64 - 1 ≈ 1.8e19 grains. Flight: (a) 40,000 (b) 34,000 (c) 30,000 = lower bound 5 x 6,000. Dozers: greedy 5+45+55+85 = 190; optimal 45+35+55+15 = 150; (190-150)/190 ≈ 21%. Arbitrary assignment 1A 2B 3C 4D = 255 (Excel). Truck: 7+10+3+14+6 = 40 (5 items, binary Solver run); minimise items: 14+17+9 = 40 (3 items); forgetting binary gave ~5.7 copies of one item. Airline: p* = a/(2b), Q* = a/2, R* = a^2/(4b).

modules.plan: Module 'Formulating correctly' (S2–S3). Cheat cards: decision variable vs parameter; the three parts (variables, objective, constraints) with units; when non-negativity applies (hours can't be recovered; materials could; portfolio shorting allows negatives — decide from the use case); Excel Solver recipe (yellow decision cells, SUMPRODUCT with $ refs, LHS <= RHS, Make Unconstrained Variables Non-Negative, Simplex LP, Sensitivity Report); furniture LP in full; Merton Truck data table and the correct contribution objective. Notes/analogies: Merton Profit A (apportioned, -1205 x1 + 2070 x2) vs Profit B (contribution 3000 x1 + 5000 x2 - 8.6M); 'test any profit expression at zero output — fixed cost doesn't vanish'; A and B agree only at the apportioning point (1000,1500); Delhi–Indore flight: 4,200x vs 200x + 4 lakh agree only at x = 100; 'garbage in, garbage out'; 'resolving the conflict is 80–90% of the job'; the swap argument (−1 Model 102, +2 Model 101: +1000 per swap, 500 swaps limited by metal stamping, +0.5M) and its three drawbacks; 'don't add capacity before solving optimally' — the apparent bottlenecks (EA, A102) are not the binding ones at the optimum (EA, MS). ONE widget: 'Profit A vs Profit B' chart for the flight example AND Merton (preset buttons). Flight: x = passengers 0–100, two lines 4200x and 200x + 400000, they cross only at x = 100; slider moves x and readout shows both costs and the gap. Merton preset: move along the line from (0,0) to (1000,1500) to (2000,1000)? Simpler: slider scales production t·(1000,1500) for t in 0–2, plot both profit expressions vs t; they meet only at t = 1. Verdict says which is right and why (test at zero). Worked problems: furniture LP (30, 40, 410 with binding check); Merton swap (+0.5M to (2000,1000)); Model 101 contribution 39000 − 24000 − 4000 − 8000 = 3000.

Module 'Graphical method and why corners' (S4–S5). One line: the S9 quiz is pen-and-paper and will ask the graphical method. Cheat cards: graphical recipe (intercepts, test the origin for the feasible side, shade, list corners by solving pairs of lines, evaluate Z); Method 1 corner enumeration (bounded region), Method 2 iso-objective line (slide parallel in the improving direction until it is about to leave the region — it always leaves at a corner), alternate optima (objective parallel to an edge: the whole edge is optimal, Solver reports one corner); definitions: solution / feasible / optimal, convex set, convex combination λxP + (1−λ)xQ, extreme point; Theorem 1 (LP region convex, the λ / 1−λ proof), Theorem 2 (if an optimum exists, a corner is optimal — weighted-average argument: Z of the midpoint of BC = average of Z(B), Z(C) = 9M), Theorem 3 (convex problem: local = global) → Method 3 (stop at a corner better than its neighbours = simplex idea); convex function / set / problem (min f s.t. g_i <= 0 with convex f, g_i); every LP is convex; 'non-convexity, not non-linearity, makes problems hard'; infeasible and unbounded LPs. Notes: the four 1-D pictures (S5: min bowl easy, max bowl hard, max concave easy, wavy hard); dented polygon where local search stops at C but E is better; e^{-x} convex with no minimiser. THE CENTREPIECE WIDGET 'Graphical LP lab' (SVG chart): presets Merton (x1 0–3000, x2 0–2000 with lines EA x1+2x2=4000, MS 2x1+2x2=6000, A101 x1=2500, A102 x2=1500) and Furniture (x1 0–70, x2 0–90; 4x1+3x2=240, 2x1+x2=100). Draw each constraint line labelled, shade the feasible polygon, dot and label corners A–F with a corner table (coordinates, Z, optimal row highlighted). A slider 'iso-profit level Z' moves the dashed objective line parallel from 0 to past the optimum; the part of the line inside the region is drawn solid; readout says how many feasible points remain on the line; at the optimum the verdict says 'last feasible point: corner D (2000, 1000), Z = 11M'; beyond it 'no feasible point on this line'. A step-through mode is NOT needed; the slider is the animation. Also expose window.__recap.m3 = {corners(preset), Z(preset, pt)}. Worked problems: Merton corner table by hand (all 6 corners); midpoint of BC weighted-average check; why maximising a bowl on an interval is hard.
modules.facts: Merton corners (label as in S4): A (0,0) Z=0; B (0,1500) 7.5M; C (1000,1500) 10.5M; D (2000,1000) 11.0M OPTIMAL (EA ∩ MS); E (2500,500) 10.0M (MS ∩ A101); F (2500,0) 7.5M. Intercepts: EA (4000,0),(0,2000); MS (3000,0),(0,3000); A101 x1=2500; A102 x2=1500. Iso line Z=7.5M passes through F and B. Midpoint of BC = (500,1500), Z = 9M = average of 7.5M and 10.5M. Furniture corners: (0,0)=0, (50,0)=350, (30,40)=410 optimal, (0,80)=400; intercepts woodwork (60,0),(0,80); painting (50,0),(0,100). Both verified with scipy linprog.

modules.plan: Module 'Sensitivity analysis' (S5–S7), all on Merton Truck. Cheat cards: binding vs non-binding (slack 0 vs > 0, non-binding shadow price 0); shadow price definition (change in optimal Z per +1 RHS) and the δ-method (keep binding constraints as equations with +δ1, +δ2, solve, substitute: Z = 11,000,000 + 2000δ1 + 500δ2); additivity (δ1=1, δ2=2 → +3000); RHS ranging = the range over which the same constraints stay binding, done graphically (slide EA line until D′ hits a neighbouring corner) or algebraically (require every x and slack >= 0); objective-coefficient ranging (objective ratio between binding-constraint ratios 1/2 and 2/2; reciprocal step for c2); reduced cost (= contribution − resources at shadow prices; basic variables have 0; the objective change per forced unit, or how much the coefficient must improve); the full Solver sensitivity table. Notes/analogies: overtime negotiation 'pay a premium up to $2,000/hour above the regular wage, within 500 hours' (S5); renting engine assembly from an outside supplier (S6); Model 103 priced out at 2350 vs contribution 2000 → reduced cost −350, launch only if contribution >= 2350 (S6); overtime decision: (2000 − 600) × 500 = 0.7M < 0.75M extra fixed overhead → no overtime, and the two formulations (overtime-hours variable y; separate regular/overtime production) (S6); origin of 'reduced cost' in Dantzig's diet problem — the price milk must be reduced by before it enters the diet (S7); 'one LP solve plus its sensitivity report answers many what-ifs without re-optimising'. TWO widgets (or one panel with two modes): (a) 'Move a constraint': choose EA or MS, slider for the RHS (EA 3000–5000, MS 4500–7500); redraw the Merton region and the optimal point sliding; table/readout: optimal (x1,x2), Z, binding set, current shadow price; inside the allowable range the verdict is teal 'same binding pair, shadow price 2000 holds'; outside it turns amber with the new binding pair (e.g. EA > 4500 → MS and A102 bind; EA < 3500 → A101 and MS/EA). Use window.__recap.m4.solve(rhsEA, rhsMS, c1, c2) implementing exact 2-D corner enumeration. (b) 'Rotate the objective': slider for c1 (1500–6500) or c2 (2000–7000) with the other fixed; draw the iso-profit line through the current optimum and highlight the optimal corner; verdict states D stays optimal for 2500 <= c1 <= 5000 / 3000 <= c2 <= 6000 and names the corner it jumps to outside. Worked problems: δ-method derivation; MS allowable range algebraically (the four-row table); Model 103 pricing out; overtime 0.7M vs 0.75M.
modules.facts: Merton optimum (2000,1000), Z = 11,000,000; slacks s1=0, s2=0, s3=1000, s4=1500. Shadow prices: EA 2000, MS 500, A101 0, A102 0. δ-method: x1 = 2000 − δ1 + δ2; x2 = 1000 + δ1 − δ2/2; Z = 11M + 2000δ1 + 500δ2. EA RHS: allowable +500/−500 → valid 3500–4500; at 4500 optimum (1500,1500) Z = 12M; above 4500 the optimum stays (1500,1500) (MS and A102 bind; EA shadow price 0); at 3500 optimum (2500,500) Z = 10M; below 3500 A101 and EA bind (shadow price of EA becomes 2500). MS RHS: +500/−1000 → valid 5000–6500; at 6500 optimum (2500,750) Z = 11.25M; at 5000 optimum (1000,1500) Z = 10.5M. MS algebra: x1 = 2000 + Δ2, x2 = 1000 − Δ2/2; s3 = 1000 − 2Δ2 >= 0 → Δ2 <= 500; s4 = 1500 + 1.5Δ2 >= 0 → Δ2 >= −1000. Non-binding: allowable increase ∞, decrease 1000 (A101) and 1500 (A102). Extra EA hour: Z = 11,002,000, mix (1999, 1001). Objective ranging: c1 in [2500, 5000] (−500/+2000): at 5001 optimum jumps to E (2500,500); below 2500 to C (1000,1500). c2 in [3000, 6000] (−2000/+1000): above 6000 jumps to C (1000,1500); below 3000 to E (2500,500). Model 103: contribution 2000; EA 0.8 h, MS 1.5 h, A101 line 1 h; opportunity cost 0.8·2000 + 1.5·500 + 1·0 = 2350; reduced cost −350 (forcing x3 = 1 lowers Z by exactly 350; LP re-solve keeps x3 = 0). Overtime: premium 50% of 1200/h = 600/h; net 1400/h × 500 h = 700,000 < 750,000 extra fixed overhead → no. Formulation 1 (y = overtime hours, −600y, EA <= 4000 + y, y <= 2000): optimum (1500, 1500, y = 500), Z = 11.7M. Formulation 2 (overtime contributions 2400 and 3800, overtime EA <= 2000): Z = 11.7M too; the regular/overtime split is not unique. Diet problem: min Σ c_j x_j s.t. L_i <= Σ a_ij x_j <= U_i, x >= 0.

modules.plan: Module 'Red Brand Canners' (S7–S8). Cheat cards: case facts (3M lb at 18¢, 20% A rating 9, 80% B rating 5; minimum ratings whole 8, juice 6, paste 5; lb/case 18/20/25; demand in cases 800k/50k/80k; offer 80k lb A at 25.5¢); sunk-cost test 'if I produce nothing, does this cost disappear?' → tomato cost excluded from contribution; blending by weighted average / alligation (whole A:B >= 3:1 i.e. >= 75% A; juice >= 1:3 i.e. >= 25% A; paste no constraint) and linearising ratios (xA1 − 3xB1 >= 0; 3xA2 − xB2 >= 0); the 6-variable LP with 7 constraints (units: $/case ÷ lb/case = $/lb; demand cases × lb/case); optimum and sensitivity results; demand <= in a max problem is fine (in a min problem it would give 'produce nothing'). Notes/analogies: Cooper (Exhibit 2, average 18¢ for every lb) vs Myers (Exhibit 3, cost proportional to quality points: A 27.93¢, B 15.52¢) — 'both are wrong': Cooper ignores that A is scarce, Myers apportions a sunk cost and his logic spirals (drop whole tomatoes → juice looks unprofitable → grade A thrown away) (S7); the expensive expert left on the bench because every product manager refuses to be billed for their hours (S7); apportioning fixed overhead may be fine for long-term strategy, never for short-term operational decisions (S7); the +100 lb puzzle: why A is worth 27.1¢ when no product earns more than 24.67¢/lb — whole tomatoes +150 lb, juice −50 lb (S8); Myers' near-match for grade A is a coincidence; grade B is worth more (17.3¢) than Myers thought (S8); the student question about juice demand: not the bottleneck (S8). ONE widget: 'Blend slider' — slider for the share of grade A in a pound of product (0–100%); show the blended rating as a weighted-average bar on a 1–10 scale with tick marks at 5, 6, 8 and three badges (whole tomatoes needs 8: needs >= 75% A; juice needs 6: >= 25% A; paste needs 5: any) turning teal/rust; plus show the cost per case under Cooper vs Myers for the chosen product preset? Keep it to the rating + a static three-way comparison table (Cooper / Myers / shadow price) outside the widget. Worked problems: derive 3:1 by alligation and by algebra; the LP's grade-A shadow price decision on the 80k lb offer (buy, gain ≈ $1,280); the paste marketing budget (reject 5¢ per extra lb since 5 > 4.83).
modules.facts: Supply A 600,000 lb, B 2,400,000 lb; total cost 3M × 0.18 = $540,000 (sunk). Contribution excluding fruit: whole $4.44/case ÷ 18 = $0.2467/lb; juice $3.96/case ÷ 20 = $0.198/lb; paste $5.55/case ÷ 25 = $0.222/lb. Demand in lb: whole 14,400,000; juice 1,000,000; paste 2,000,000. Optimum (verified scipy): xA1 = 525,000, xB1 = 175,000 (whole total 700,000 lb); xA2 = 75,000, xB2 = 225,000 (juice 300,000 lb); xA3 = 0, xB3 = 2,000,000 (paste); total contribution ≈ $676,067; profit after the sunk $540,000 ≈ $136,067. Shadow prices: grade A supply 0.2710 $/lb (27.1¢); grade B 0.1737 (17.3¢ — the lecture says 17.3); whole and juice demand 0; paste demand 0.0483 $/lb (4.83¢); the two quality (>=) constraints about −0.0243 each (not discussed in class). +100 lb A: contribution +$27.10; whole +150 lb, juice −50 lb: 150 × 0.2467 − 50 × 0.198 = 37.0 − 9.9 = 27.1. Allowable increase of grade A supply = 600,000 lb (shadow price 0.271 holds up to 1,200,000 lb). 80,000 lb at 25.5¢: gain 80,000 × 0.271 = 21,680 vs cost 20,400 → net ≈ +$1,280 → buy. Reduced cost of xA3 ≈ −0.0973 $/lb (−0.097); adding 0.098 to its coefficient makes it enter and whole-tomato production drops to zero. Myers: Z·600k·9/5… solve 600,000 a + 2,400,000 b = 540,000 with a = 1.8 b → b = 0.1552, a = 0.2793 $/lb. Myers fruit cost/case: whole 18(0.75·0.2793 + 0.25·0.1552) ≈ 4.47; juice ≈ 3.72; paste 25·0.1552 ≈ 3.88. Cooper fruit cost/case: 3.24 / 3.60 / 4.50. Whole tomatoes under Cooper: price 12.00, variable cost 10.80 → contribution 1.20; under Myers ≈ 4.44 − 4.47 = −0.03. Blending: rating(p) = 9p + 5(1 − p) where p = share of A; >= 8 ⇔ p >= 0.75; >= 6 ⇔ p >= 0.25; >= 5 always.

modules.plan: Module 'Shadow-price signs, duality, and an introduction to IP' (S8–S9). Cheat cards: the principle 'region expands → optimum can't worsen; shrinks → can't improve'; RHS +1 on <= expands, on >= shrinks, on = shifts; the full sign table (max: <= ≥0, >= ≤0, = unrestricted; min: <= ≤0, >= ≥0, = unrestricted) and 'standard constraints' (<= for max, >= for min) have non-negative shadow prices; primal–dual: shadow prices of the primal are the dual's variables; conversion rules (max↔min, RHS↔objective coefficients, transpose, standard↔standard, non-standard↔non-standard, unrestricted variable↔equality constraint); which to solve (graphical: the 2-variable one; simplex: the one with fewer constraints — 2 vars/30 constraints primal becomes 32 vars/30 equations, the dual 32 vars/2 equations); both primal and dual feasible at a point → optimal; ILP/MILP definition, uses (counts, binary decisions: knapsack, capital budgeting, facility location; either–or, if–then, bin packing), LP vs IP picture (lattice points; the LP corner is often not integer), bounds max Z_LP >= Z_IP, min Z_LP <= Z_IP. Notes/analogies: the 'smelly / reactive' resource you are forced to use up (x2 = 4 equality) with shadow price −19 (S8); 'buy my resources' story for the dual: you offer prices u1, u2 that make producing not worth my while, and minimise what you pay (S9). ONE widget: 'Primal → dual stepper' using Player (.viz-body with pre.pcode showing the primal, the dual being built in the stage, .vars). States walk the S9 messy example: (0) show the primal min problem; (1) signs of u1 (C1 >= in min: standard → u1 >= 0), (2) u2 (C2 <= in min → u2 <= 0), (3) u3 (C3 = → unrestricted); (4) dual objective max 40u1 + 80u2 + 50u3 (primal RHS); (5–8) one dual constraint per primal variable column with its sign from the variable's sign: x1 >= 0 → <= −4; x2 <= 0 → >= 8; x3 unrestricted → = −5; x4 >= 0 → <= 1; (9) the finished dual. Highlight the primal column being transposed (amber) and the dual line being written (teal). Then a second preset: the S9 product-mix primal (max 8x1+4x2+5x3, two <= constraints) → dual (min 18u1+11u2, three >= constraints, u >= 0) with the buy-my-resources caption; and state both optimal values equal 47. Worked problems: the S8 equality example (u2 = −19 from 124 → 105); write the dual of the product-mix primal.
modules.facts: S8 example: max 20x1 + x2 s.t. x1 + x2 <= 10, x2 <= 4, x >= 0 → optimum (10,0), Z = 200, u1 = 20, u2 = 0; corners (0,0)=0, (0,4)=4, (6,4)=124, (10,0)=200. With x2 = 4 as equality: optimum (6,4), Z = 124; RHS 11 → (7,4) Z = 144 (u1 = 20); x2 = 5 → (5,5) Z = 105 → u2 = −19. S9 product mix: max 8x1 + 4x2 + 5x3 s.t. 3x1 + 5x2 + 2x3 <= 18, 2x1 + 3x2 + x3 <= 11, x >= 0 → optimum x = (4, 0, 3), Z = 47, shadow prices u = (2, 1). Dual: min 18u1 + 11u2 s.t. 3u1 + 2u2 >= 8, 5u1 + 3u2 >= 4, 2u1 + u2 >= 5, u >= 0 → u = (2, 1), W = 47 (scipy-verified; the lecture promised but did not compute this). Messy primal: min −4x1 + 8x2 − 5x3 + x4 s.t. C1: 3x1 − 2x2 + 6x3 − x4 >= 40; C2: 2x1 + 3x2 − 5x3 + 2x4 <= 80; C3: 3x1 − 5x2 + x3 + 2x4 = 50; x1 >= 0, x2 <= 0, x3 unrestricted, x4 >= 0 (RHS 40, 80, 50 and rows 2–3 reconstructed from the dual the lecturer wrote). Dual: max 40u1 + 80u2 + 50u3 s.t. 3u1 + 2u2 + 3u3 <= −4; −2u1 + 3u2 − 5u3 >= 8; 6u1 − 5u2 + u3 = −5; −u1 + 2u2 + 2u3 <= 1; u1 >= 0, u2 <= 0, u3 unrestricted (the transcript said '<= −1' for the last line; the correct RHS is +1).
